questions.text: What can be inferred from the emergence of AI in education?

options.text: It completely removes ethical concerns and academic misconduct issues.

questions.explanationHtml: Thông tin: While they can support learning, they also make undetectable dishonesty increasingly plausible. A sai ở "completely removes"; C sai ở "without negative consequences"; D sai ở "eliminates" (bài đọc nói cần định nghĩa lại tính liêm chính).

questions.explanationHtml: Thông tin: AI tools can generate essays... While they can support learning... → "they" chỉ "AI tools".

clusters.text: Preparing students for the job market is one of the main goals of modern education. Schools should not only provide academic knowledge but also help students develop practical skills. For example, students need communication skills, teamwork, and problem-solving abilities to succeed in the workplace. In addition, basic digital skills are important because many jobs today require the use of technology. Schools can organize career guidance programs, internships, and workshops to give students real experience. Learning how to write a CV and perform well in a job interview is also useful. When students understand what employers expect, they can prepare themselves better. As a result, they will feel more confident and ready to enter the job market after graduation.

School uniforms remain a common requirement in many education systems. Supporters argue that uniforms promote equality by reducing visible differences in wealth and fashion. When students wear the same clothes, they may feel a stronger sense of belonging and school identity. Uniforms can also create a more disciplined learning environment and reduce distractions related to appearance. In addition, parents often find them practical and cost-effective in the long term.
However, some people believe that school uniforms are outdated. They argue that clothing is a form of self-expression, especially for teenagers who are developing their identities. Strict dress codes may limit creativity and individuality. Moreover, uniforms do not automatically solve deeper issues such as bullying or academic pressure. All in all, whether uniforms are necessary or outdated depends on how schools balance discipline with personal freedom.

Education is widely considered a fundamental human right. Supporters of free education argue that every individual, regardless of economic background, deserves equal access to learning opportunities. When governments provide free schooling, they reduce social inequality and give disadvantaged students a fair chance to succeed. An educated population also contributes to economic growth, social stability, and democratic participation. From this perspective, free education is not simply a benefit but a long-term investment in national development.
On the other hand, some believe that education can be seen as a privilege due to limited public resources. Governments must allocate funding carefully, and maintaining high-quality free education requires significant financial commitment. In certain contexts, families who can afford tuition may be expected to contribute. Nevertheless, many argue that while advanced or specialized programs may involve costs, basic education should remain accessible to all as a universal right.

In reality, most students spend years in school without ever being taught how to learn. They memorize formulas, underline key words, and revise the night before exams. They chase grades, not understanding. But have you ever asked yourself why you forget most of what you studied just a few months later? Many learners are trained to absorb information quickly and reproduce it on paper. Once the test is over, the knowledge quietly disappears. Is that really education, or just short-term survival?
Learning how to learn means understanding your own thinking process. It involves questioning ideas, connecting concepts, and reflecting on mistakes. Real learning happens when you can explain a topic in your own words and apply it in a new situation. It is less about collecting facts and more about building insight. So, next time you open a textbook, ask yourself: are you studying for a grade, or are you actually learning something meaningful?

Before the widespread use of the Internet, academic dishonesty was limited by physical constraints. Students who wished to cheat often relied on handwritten notes hidden in exam rooms, copied homework from classmates, or secretly exchanged answers during tests. Plagiarism required access to printed books or libraries, which made it more time-consuming and easier to detect. Although cheating certainly existed, it demanded effort and carried a higher risk of being caught. Information was not instantly accessible, and academic misconduct was relatively restricted in scale.
With the arrival of the Internet, the landscape changed dramatically. Students gained immediate access to countless online sources, essays, and answer keys. Copying and pasting became effortless, and contract cheating services began offering customized assignments for a fee. The digital environment blurred the boundaries between research and plagiarism, making misconduct both more convenient and more difficult to monitor. Educational institutions have since had to adopt plagiarism-detection software and stricter policies.
Now, the rise of artificial intelligence introduces a new ethical dilemma. AI tools can generate essays, solve complex problems, and imitate academic writing styles within seconds. While they can support learning, they also make undetectable dishonesty increasingly plausible. The challenge today is not merely preventing cheating, but redefining academic integrity in an age where machines can think alongside students.
